title: Three canons, one teacher
hookLine: the Pali canon, the Chinese canon and the Tibetan canon
carry: the teaching itself is the teacher

lines: THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.
THEY REMEMBERED, THEN WROTE IT DOWN.
cards: Near the end of his life, in the Pali account of his last days, the Buddha sees a worry coming. When he is gone, someone will say: our teacher is finished, we have no teacher anymore. Not so, he tells Ananda.
The teaching and the discipline he has given them will be their teacher. So the monks did what people do with a teacher they cannot afford to lose. They remembered.
They recited together. Later, the words were written down, and in different lands the remembering took different shapes.

teach.b: A canon is a collection a community treats as its scripture. Buddhists keep three great ones, each in its own language, each with its own shape.
First, the Pali canon, kept by the Theravada schools of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
Its name is the Tipitaka, which tradition explains as three baskets: one for the monastic discipline, one for the discourses, one for the higher teaching called Abhidhamma.
Theravada tradition says it was handed down by memory for a long time before it was written.
Second, the Chinese canon, sometimes called the great storehouse of scriptures.

It holds texts translated from Indian languages, including collections of early discourses called the Agamas, which run close to the Pali ones: lay the two side by side and you find the same story, told with small differences.
It also holds Mahayana sutras, monastic codes, and works first written in China, such as yesterday's Platform Sutra. It was read across China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
Third, the Tibetan canon, which you met in year three, in two parts.

teach.h: TIBETAN: THE WORD AND THE COMMENTS.
teach.b: The Kangyur gathers what Tibetan tradition counts as the Buddha's own word, in translation. The Tengyur gathers commentaries and treatises by later Indian teachers. Tibetan translators worked closely from Indian texts.
The three overlap far more than their covers suggest.

teach.h: THREE SHELVES, THE SAME FOUR TRUTHS.
teach.b: A monk in Bangkok, a nun in Taipei and a lama in Dharamsala can each open their own canon and find the Buddha teaching the four truths.
The wording differs. The bookshelves differ.

how: Theravada communities study and chant from the Pali canon, East Asian Buddhists draw on the Chinese canon, and Tibetan and Himalayan Buddhists use the Kangyur and Tengyur, often keeping the volumes wrapped in cloth on the temple shelf.

o: three sermons the Buddha gave in his final days
the Pali, Chinese and Tibetan collections of scripture
three councils that settled every dispute for good

p: early discourses in the Chinese canon

s: the three canons share no teachings at all
they overlap: all three hold the Buddha teaching the four truths, in different words.
in the Pali account of his last days, the Buddha says the teaching will be the teacher
he tells Ananda the teaching and discipline will be their teacher after he is gone.
the Chinese canon holds only texts written in China
it holds many translations from Indian languages, along with works first written in China.

games.q: you're Ananda. the Buddha is near the end of his life, and some fear they'll have no teacher. what does he tell you?
o: choose a new teacher to lead you.
the teaching and discipline will be your teacher.
wait for the next Buddha to come.
games.why: he names no successor. the teaching itself is to be the teacher, and the canons are how communities kept it.

practice: Name the three canons quietly, one to a breath: the Pali, read this morning in a monastery in Sri Lanka or Thailand; the Chinese, a page turning in Seoul or Kyoto; the Tibetan, a long cloth-wrapped book being unwrapped on a table.
Then sit with the thought the Buddha left Ananda: the teaching itself as the teacher.

wordCard.voice: Three canons. The Pali, the Chinese and the Tibetan collections of scripture, each its own library, often holding the same teachings in different words. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Tipitaka, the name of the Pali canon, which tradition explains as three baskets.

carryVoice: Your line: the teaching itself is the teacher. Three canons, three shelves, one teacher. Until tomorrow.
